title: Rachel weeping (Matthew 2:13–23)
hookLine: Herod's massacre, and Rachel refusing to be comforted (Jeremiah 31:15)
tomorrow: is saying sorry enough, or does it have to show?

cards: A memory pops up on a phone years after a loss, and under it the comments still say, so sorry. Grief doesn't keep to a calendar. Here's an odd detail in Matthew.

Rachel, Jacob's wife, a mother from Genesis, has been gone since the Bible's first book. Yet in Matthew's second chapter, near Bethlehem, she is weeping. Why is a woman from Genesis crying in the Christmas story?
This is a hard page, and it's told gently.

teach.b: First, what happens. Warned in another dream, Joseph takes the child and his mother by night into Egypt.
Herod, seeing the wise men won't come back, "sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under."
Matthew says it in one plain sentence and doesn't hurry past it. Now the puzzle.

Matthew reaches for the prophet Jeremiah: "In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not."
And Genesis says where Rachel lies.

teach.h: BURIED ON THE WAY TO BETHLEHEM.
teach.b: She died giving birth on the road, and "was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem." So Matthew hears the mother buried beside Bethlehem crying for the town's children. Notice the phrase: would not be comforted.

Nobody scolds her. Nobody offers a reason that makes the loss make sense. One to tell a friend tonight: in Jeremiah, the very next line turns to hope, "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears."
He quotes only the weeping, and lets the mothers' grief stand at the start of his Gospel.

how: Some churches keep a feast of the Holy Innocents in the Christmas season, remembering the children of Bethlehem and, often, children who suffer today.

he quotes Rachel, who "would not be comforted," and stops before Jeremiah's next line of hope.

games.q: a coworker's mom died last month. at lunch someone says, "you've got to stay positive, she'd want you smiling." your coworker goes quiet. what fits Matthew's page?
o: sit with her and say you're sorry, with no reason attached.
agree, and add that every loss happens for a reason.
change the subject to something cheerful to help.
games.why: Matthew offers no reason that makes the loss make sense. Rachel would not be comforted, and the text lets her grieve.

practice: Listen for the quietest sound in the room, a fan, a clock, your own breath, and let it stand for mothers who are grieving: one you know, or ones you'll never meet. Don't hurry them toward comfort.
If you pray, you can hold them before God in your own words or with none; and if grief or danger feels close to you right now, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
